draft.title: Atomic absorption spectroscopy
card: Atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS) finds the concentration of a metal in a sample. It can measure very low concentrations, such as traces of lead in water.
The sample is turned into a cloud of free atoms, usually in a flame. A lamp containing the metal being tested shines light of one set wavelength through the cloud.
Atoms of that metal absorb some of this light. The more atoms there are, the more light is absorbed.

The absorbance of the sample is compared with the absorbance of standard solutions of known concentration. This gives the concentration in the sample. AAS was developed in Australia, by Alan Walsh and his team at CSIRO.
draft.remember: AAS: more atoms in the flame means more light absorbed, so absorbance shows concentration.

a.q: In AAS, what is measured to find the concentration of a metal?
opts: How much light of a set wavelength the atoms absorb
How much mass of precipitate the metal forms
The colour the metal gives to a flame
How much heat the sample gives out
a.why: Free atoms of the metal absorb light of a set wavelength, and more atoms absorb more light. Flame colour is a different test, and AAS does not weigh a precipitate.
a.clue: The name of the method says what the atoms do to the light.

b.q: A lab tests river water for copper using AAS. Sample A absorbs more light than sample B at the copper wavelength. What does this show?
opts: Sample A has a higher copper concentration
Sample A has a lower copper concentration
Sample A contains no other metals
Sample B has more light shining through the lamp
b.why: More absorbed light means more copper atoms in the light path, so sample A has more copper. The reverse would mean less absorption, not more.
b.clue: More atoms in the flame means more light taken in.

a.best: How much light of a set wavelength the atoms absorb

b.best: Sample A has a higher copper concentration
